source.title: A Tale of Tails: Model Collapse as a Change of Scaling Laws
source.authors: Elvis Dohmatob; Yunzhen Feng; Pu Yang; François Charton; Julia Kempe

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests delayed improvement in a different setting and with different measures: test loss and emergence of previously unlearnable GCD skills as training sample size increases.
record.gate_note: The paper reports grokking-like curves for mixtures of clean and AI-generated data in GCD transformers and Llama2 fine-tuning. The GCD results below are from Table 4; the paper describes these as delayed learning, but does not report training accuracy saturation or test accuracy moving from chance to near-perfect. Llama mixture results are described in the text, but their plotted values are not numerically stated. Other model-collapse and scaling results that do not report delayed generalization are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper's 'grokking' is a different construct from any claim version. It is a plateau in test error as sample size grows, caused by tail-cut AI data, which ends once clean data covers the tail (length of order k^β/π). GCD and Llama runs train on growing streams of fresh samples, so there is no fixed small training set, no train-accuracy saturation and no memorize-then-generalize gap. None of V1–V7 is tested. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely right but should make clear what 'grokking' means here. Training on AI data with cut or narrowed tails stops scaling and loses skills. Mixing in even a small fraction π of clean data ends the test-error plateau after about k^β/π samples, and the authors call this grokking. They report it in GCD transformers (Table 4, where they say delay grows with AI fraction) and as a smoothed version in Llama2 fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines model-collapse effects from synthetic-data tail changes and data mixtures, using scaling with sample size, test loss/perplexity, and GCD skill acquisition rather than the original grokking setup. It does not test grokking from small clean algorithmic datasets alone.
record.method_sensitivity: GCD outcomes and delay vary with the AI-data mixture fraction and arithmetic base. Llama2 fine-tuning results use top-pinf = 0.9 and temperature τ = 0.9; the paper also reports other generation settings elsewhere, but they are not rows for these delayed-generalization results.

fits_no_version.finding: In GCD transformers trained on streamed clean/AI mixtures, new GCDs that AI-only training cannot learn appear after a delay. Success falls with AI fraction (0/10 at 73%). Delays are non-monotonic: base 2023 is 567M clean vs 530M at 9% AI; base 1000 is 190M at 50% AI.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixing tail-cut synthetic data with clean data yields a test-loss plateau over sample size whose length grows with the synthetic fraction (k^β/π).

fits_no_version.finding: Llama2-7B LoRA fine-tuning on Wikitext-103 with 2% (Figure 7) or 10% (Figure 34) original data mixed into generated data shows perplexity plateau-then-decline curves. These are shown in figures only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Same mixture-plateau ('grokking' in the authors' sense) in LLM fine-tuning on synthetic/clean mixtures.

record.problems: The GCD delayed-learning results are aggregate counts over 10 experiments and do not report training accuracy or a chance-to-near-perfect test-accuracy transition. The Llama2 mixture results are shown only in figures, without numerical values or reported uncertainty. The Llama experiment is fine-tuning on a particular Wikitext-derived task, not a broad test of realistic pretraining.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional model-collapse and scaling curves for Hutter models, bigram models, GCD clean-versus-AI training, and Llama generations. These were left out because they do not report delayed generalization of the kind named in the tested versions, or they measure collapse without a delayed recovery. Results cited from other studies were also excluded.

untested.parts: Train-accuracy saturation, a chance-to-near-perfect test jump, and a delay growing as the training set shrinks: nothing here uses a fixed small dataset.
Not tested: no circuit analysis or progress measures.
Not tested: no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
Not tested: the Llama curves are sample-size plateaus from synthetic-data mixing, not delayed generalization after fitting.
Not tested: no weight decay, critical dataset size or ungrokking.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1/V4 'tests' and its supports labels are wrong: the term grokking is reused for a scaling-law plateau, not the train/test gap of the original sources. Table 4 also has a clean (0%) row (465/243, 530/567, 1180/520 M) that serves as the comparison baseline and is not recorded. Footnote 7 says runs stopped near 3B samples, so the 0/10 results at 73% AI may be censored.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test small training sets, training accuracy saturation, a chance-to-near-perfect test-accuracy jump, or whether shrinking the training set increases optimization delay. The GCD experiments use large numbers of examples and mixtures of correct and AI-generated data; their reported outcomes are delayed skill acquisition and test loss.
No mechanistic circuit, Fourier algorithm, memorizing component, or continuous progress measure is analyzed.
No initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation, or lazy-to-rich transition, is tested.

The study tests Llama2-7B fine-tuning on Wikitext-103-derived data, including AI-generated-data mixtures. It does not test pretraining or establish that the effect occurs broadly across realistic training regimes.
The study does not test weight decay, low-norm circuit selection, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below such a size.
The study does not compare whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
The study does not test whether optimizer or numerical artifacts cause the delay.
